claims.text: Dynamic deformation in equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed primarily by dislocation glide through composition-induced solid-solution obstacles.
Atomic-size mismatches among Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn produce local lattice distortions.
These local lattice distortions create a heterogeneous dislocation glide-resistance landscape.
The lattice-distortion landscape controls thermal activation barriers at low temperatures.
The lattice-distortion landscape controls the extent of dynamic solute pinning at high temperatures.
At cryogenic temperatures, reduced phonon damping allows dislocation inertial effects to become significant.
Dislocation inertial effects contribute to a steep cryogenic increase in CRSS.
The cryogenic CRSS increase should level off at very low temperatures when inertial effects dominate.
At elevated temperatures, increased diffusivity of Mn and Fe enables dynamic solute pinning.
Short-range Mn- and Fe-containing solute atmospheres form and dynamically break around moving dislocations.
Dynamic solute pinning produces Portevin-Le Chatelier-type serrated flow at elevated temperatures.
Dynamic solute pinning produces a modest elevated-temperature CRSS increase.
Local lattice distortion alone, without Co, governs the strength-ductility balance across the stated temperature and strain-rate regimes.
The applicable material is equiatomic, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn produced by controlled solidification and homogenization.
Compression testing should cover approximately 10 K to 1073 K at an engineering strain rate near 1×10^-4 s^-1.
Strain-rate jumps from 1×10^-4 to 1×10^-2 s^-1 near 10% strain are proposed to measure changes in apparent activation volume.
TEM-observed slip-band patterns and local dislocation arrangements should correlate with the temperature-dependent mechanical trends.
Analogous studies in related high-entropy alloys support a role for local lattice distortions in controlling dislocation motion.

contradictions.description: Dislocation inertia is described as intensifying the cryogenic CRSS increase, but inertial dominance is also invoked to explain leveling off of CRSS at the lowest temperatures; the direction of the proposed inertial contribution is therefore internally unclear.

The elevated-temperature CRSS increment is variously compared with an intermediate-temperature baseline and with the room-temperature baseline, so the reference condition for falsification is inconsistent.
